stops.title: The Reichstag and the Airlift
stops.text: You're standing in front of the Reichstag, and in 1948 this lawn was the stage for the first battle of the Cold War. After the war, Berlin sat deep inside the Soviet zone, divided into four sectors. In June 1948 the Western Allies introduced a new currency, the Deutsche Mark, and Stalin answered by cutting every road, rail line and canal into West Berlin. Two million people were suddenly an island. The West chose not to fight its way in, but to fly. For almost a year, American and British planes landed in Berlin around the clock, at the peak one every few minutes, carrying food, medicine and above all coal. In total there were more than two hundred and seventy thousand flights. One American pilot, Gail Halvorsen, started dropping sweets tied to tiny handkerchief parachutes for children waiting at the airport fence, and Berliners called the planes Rosinenbomber, raisin bombers. On the ninth of September 1948, around three hundred thousand people gathered right here, in front of the burnt-out Reichstag. Mayor Ernst Reuter told them, and the world: Ihr Völker der Welt, schaut auf diese Stadt. You peoples of the world, look upon this city. In May 1949 Stalin lifted the blockade. He had lost. Now look behind the building, towards the river. When the Wall went up in 1961, it ran directly along the Spree, just behind the Reichstag, which stood in the West, silent and unused as a parliament. On the riverbank you'll find a row of white crosses. They remember people who died trying to cross this border, some of them in this very water. Next, ride south to the Brandenburg Gate. It's just a few hundred metres.

more.text: Let's stay with the airlift a little longer, because the numbers are hard to believe. When the blockade began in June 1948, the Americans called their part Operation Vittles, and the British called theirs Operation Plainfare. Nobody thought it could feed a city of two million for more than a few weeks. West Berlin needed thousands of tonnes of supplies every single day, and most of it was coal, heavy and dirty, for power stations, factories and stoves. Tempelhof and Gatow airports were not enough, so a third airport was built at Tegel in the French sector. Berliners did much of the work by hand, many of them women, and the runway was ready in about three months. The pilots flew in tight corridors over Soviet territory, landing and taking off in all weather, with barely any time on the ground between flights. The high point came at Easter 1949. In a single day and night the Allies flew almost fourteen hundred flights into Berlin, landing roughly one plane every minute. It was a show of strength, and a message to Moscow: this can go on forever. A few weeks later, Stalin gave up. By the end, the airlift had delivered more than two million tonnes of supplies. It also had a cost. Around a hundred people died, American and British aircrew and German workers, in crashes and accidents. The memorial at Tempelhof, with its three concrete arms pointing west, remembers them. The building behind you has its own story. It burned in 1933, and the Nazis used the fire as a pretext to suspend civil rights. In 1945 it was one of the last places fought over in Berlin, and a Soviet photograph of a soldier raising the red flag on its roof became one of the most famous images of the war. Soviet soldiers wrote their names on the walls inside, and some of that graffiti was kept when the building was rebuilt. In 1995 the artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrapped the whole Reichstag in silver fabric, and millions came to see it. Since 1999 the German parliament has met here again, under a glass dome you can visit for free if you book ahead. From the top you can look across the river, to where the Wall once ran.

stops.title: The Brandenburg Gate
stops.text: The Brandenburg Gate was built in the seventeen-eighties as a gate of peace. For twenty-eight years it was the most photographed symbol of division in the world. The sector border ran just to the west of where you are now. The gate itself stood in East Berlin, and after August 1961 it was sealed inside the death strip. Nobody could pass through it from either side. It became a stage for the West. In June 1963, John F. Kennedy came to look over the Wall here. East German authorities hung huge red banners between the columns so that he couldn't see into the East. He went on to Schöneberg town hall and said: Ich bin ein Berliner. Twenty-four years later, in June 1987, the rock star David Bowie played a concert on the lawn behind the Reichstag, with speakers pointing towards the East. Thousands of young East Berliners crowded near the Wall on the other side to listen, and when police moved in, they began to chant: the Wall must go. A few days later, Ronald Reagan stood right here, on the western side, and said: Mister Gorbachev, tear down this wall. Many of his own advisers had wanted that line cut from the speech. At the time, most people thought it was theatre. Two and a half years later, it happened. On the night of the ninth of November 1989, people climbed onto the Wall in front of this gate and danced on it. The gate officially reopened on the twenty-second of December 1989. Next, ride south along Ebertstrasse to Potsdamer Platz. Watch the ground as you ride: the double row of cobblestones marks exactly where the Wall used to stand.

more.text: Look up at the chariot on top of the gate. That's the Quadriga, four horses pulling the goddess of victory, made by the sculptor Johann Gottfried Schadow in the seventeen-nineties. The gate itself was designed by Carl Gotthard Langhans and modelled on the entrance to the Acropolis in Athens. The Quadriga has travelled. In 1806, after Napoleon defeated Prussia, he had it taken down and shipped to Paris as a trophy. When he was defeated in 1814, it came back to Berlin in triumph, and the goddess was given a new staff with an iron cross and a Prussian eagle. That's why the square behind the gate, on the eastern side, is called Pariser Platz, Paris Square. By 1945 the Quadriga was almost completely destroyed. What happened next is one of the strangest stories of divided Berlin. Plaster casts of the original had been made during the war and were kept in West Berlin. In 1958 a West Berlin foundry used them to make a new Quadriga in copper, and it was handed over to the East, because the gate stood in the East. East Berlin put it up, but first removed the iron cross and the eagle, which it saw as symbols of Prussian militarism. So for decades, the East German Quadriga was a West Berlin product with its symbols taken off. After reunification it was restored with the cross and eagle back in place. Now picture Pariser Platz during the division. The grand buildings around it, embassies, banks and the famous Hotel Adlon, were ruins or gone. The square was part of the border area, empty and closed to ordinary people. Almost everything you see around the square today, including the Adlon, was built after 1990, and much of it deliberately follows the old outlines. On New Year's Eve 1989, just weeks after the Wall opened, hundreds of thousands of people celebrated here. Some climbed up onto the gate itself, and the Quadriga was damaged again that night. It had to come down for repair. Today the gate is closed to cars, and you can simply walk through it, from what was West to what was East, in a few seconds. For twenty-eight years, that walk was impossible.

stops.title: Potsdamer Platz
stops.text: Look at the glass towers around you and try to imagine this: for almost thirty years, this was nothing. Sand, weeds, watchtowers and rabbits. Before the war, Potsdamer Platz was one of the busiest squares in Europe, with trams, department stores and hotels. The green tower with the clock is a replica of Europe's first traffic light tower, installed here in 1924 because the traffic was simply out of control. Bombing in 1945 destroyed most of it. Then the square became the meeting point of three sectors, American, British and Soviet. On the seventeenth of June 1953, during the East German uprising, this square was a battlefield. Protesters faced Soviet tanks here, and a building on the eastern side was set on fire. When the Wall came in 1961, it cut the square straight through. The remaining buildings were torn down to create a clear field of fire for the border guards. From observation platforms on the western side, tourists and visiting politicians would climb up and stare across the empty strip into the East. After the Wall fell, this huge empty space became the stage for something surreal. In July 1990, Roger Waters performed The Wall here, in front of around three hundred and fifty thousand people, on the former death strip itself. Then came the builders. In the nineties, Potsdamer Platz was the largest construction site in Europe. Nearly everything you see is younger than the fall of the Wall. Look for the original Wall segments near the station entrance. Next, ride east along Leipziger Strasse to the large grey government building on the corner of Wilhelmstrasse.

more.text: Here is something most of the people around you don't know: you may be standing above a ghost station. When the Wall was built, some U-Bahn and S-Bahn lines from West Berlin ran through tunnels under East Berlin. The trains were allowed to keep running, but the stations under the East were closed and sealed. West Berlin passengers rode through dim, empty platforms, with armed East German border guards watching from small posts. The trains did not stop. Berliners called them Geisterbahnhöfe, ghost stations. The S-Bahn station under Potsdamer Platz was one of them. Above ground, in the empty strip, one building held on. The Weinhaus Huth, a wine merchant's building from the early twentieth century, was built with a strong steel frame, and it survived the bombing when almost everything around it fell. For decades it stood alone on the western side of the wasteland, looking a little lost. It's still here today, surrounded by the new towers, and it now houses an art space. Another survivor was part of the Grand Hotel Esplanade, which had been one of the finest hotels in Berlin. When the Sony Center was planned in the nineties, the old breakfast room and the imperial hall of the hotel were in the way. So in 1996 engineers lifted the imperial hall, about thirteen hundred tonnes of it, and moved it some seventy-five metres on air cushions. You can see it behind glass inside the Sony Center. Why was this square so important before the war? It was a crossroads of major streets next to a big railway terminus, and traffic moved through here at all hours. There were enormous entertainment palaces, with restaurants themed on different countries, dance halls and cinemas. After 1945, it all ended up at the corner of three sectors, and the black market moved in. People traded cigarettes, coffee and nylon stockings, often in the shadow of the ruins. When the Wall came down, the land here was some of the most valuable in Europe, and huge companies bought large parts of it. Some Berliners still argue about whether the new Potsdamer Platz is a city or a shopping centre. Either way, it's a remarkable thing to see: a square that disappeared for almost thirty years, and then was built again from nothing.

stops.title: The House of Ministries and the 1953 uprising
stops.text: This massive building has lived through almost every chapter of modern German history. It was built in 1936 as Hermann Göring's Air Ministry, and it's one of the few Nazi government buildings that survived the bombing. In October 1949, the German Democratic Republic, East Germany, was founded inside this building. It then became the GDR's House of Ministries. Walk to the colonnade on the Leipziger Strasse side. You'll find a long mural made of Meissen porcelain tiles, completed in the early fifties: happy workers, farmers, families, and young people marching towards a bright socialist future. That was the official picture. Now look down at the ground in front of it. There's a large photograph under glass showing the real people who came here. On the sixteenth of June 1953, construction workers from the Stalinallee building site put down their tools and marched to this building. The government had raised their work quotas, which effectively meant a pay cut. Thousands gathered here demanding to speak to the leadership. A minister climbed onto a table to calm them, and was shouted down. By the next morning, the seventeenth of June, strikes and protests had spread to hundreds of towns across East Germany, with around a million people taking part. Their demands had moved from work quotas to free elections. The Soviet army sent in tanks, and the uprising was crushed within days. At least fifty-five people were killed. After reunification, the building had one more dark chapter. It housed the Treuhand, the agency that privatised or closed East German companies. Its head, Detlev Rohwedder, was assassinated by the Red Army Faction in 1991. Today the building is named after him, and it's the Federal Ministry of Finance. Next, go around the corner to Niederkirchnerstrasse, where a long piece of the original Wall still stands.

more.text: This building was designed by Ernst Sagebiel for the Nazi Air Ministry and finished in 1936, in record time. It has more than two thousand rooms, and it was built to impress and to intimidate: stone facades, long corridors, and an entrance courtyard made for parades. Its steel frame and heavy walls are the reason it survived the bombing almost intact. The mural you saw was made by the painter Max Lingner, and it's called Building the Republic. Lingner had lived in France for many years and wanted to paint in a freer, more colourful style. The officials made him change it again and again, until it looked the way the party wanted. It's a picture of a future that people were told to believe in, placed on the building where they came to protest. The memorial in the ground in front of it opened in 2000. It's a large photograph from the seventeenth of June 1953, showing demonstrators marching arm in arm, set into the pavement at the same size as the mural, as if to answer it. What happened after the uprising shaped Germany for decades. In the West, the day became a public holiday, the Day of German Unity, and the wide avenue through the Tiergarten was renamed Strasse des Siebzehnten Juni, the Street of the Seventeenth of June. You rode past its eastern end at the Brandenburg Gate. In the East, the uprising was officially described as a fascist provocation organised from the West, and it was not openly discussed for almost forty years. The playwright Bertolt Brecht, who lived in East Berlin, wrote a short poem about it that he never published in his lifetime. In it, he mentions a leaflet saying that the people had lost the government's confidence, and asks whether it would not be simpler for the government to dissolve the people and elect another. For the East German leadership, the lesson of 1953 was that they could not rely on their own people, only on Soviet tanks. That fear never went away. It helps explain why, when hundreds of thousands of people were leaving for the West through Berlin in the late fifties, the answer in 1961 was to build a wall.

stops.title: The Wall at Niederkirchnerstrasse
stops.text: This is one of the longest stretches of original Wall left in the city centre, around two hundred metres. Look closely at the damage. After November 1989, thousands of people came with hammers and chisels to break off souvenirs. Berliners called them Mauerspechte, wall woodpeckers. In some places they chipped so deep that you can see the steel reinforcing bars inside. That's why this piece is now protected behind a fence. What you're looking at is only one layer of the border. The Wall wasn't a single wall at all, but a strip. From the East, a person trying to escape would have to cross an inner wall, a fence with alarm wires, a sandy strip that was raked smooth to show footprints, a patrol road, floodlights, anti-vehicle trenches, dog runs, watchtowers with guards under orders to shoot, and only then this final wall, the one facing West. Its smooth, rounded top was designed so that nobody could get a grip on it. The location adds another layer of history. Before the war, this street was called Prinz-Albrecht-Strasse, and it held the headquarters of the Gestapo and the SS. The Wall was built across the ruins of the buildings where the Nazi terror was planned. The foundations and cellars were only dug up in the eighties. They're now part of the Topography of Terror documentation centre, right behind this segment. So in one glance you can see two dictatorships stacked on top of each other. Next, ride east along Zimmerstrasse to Checkpoint Charlie. You'll be riding right along the old border line.

more.text: The segments you see here belong to the later generations of the Wall. In August 1961 the first barrier was barbed wire, followed within days by walls of concrete blocks and bricks, often built by hand. Over the years it was rebuilt and improved several times. The final version, used from the mid seventies, was made of prefabricated L-shaped concrete segments, each about three and a half metres tall and weighing a few tonnes. They could be set up quickly by crane, and tens of thousands of them were used. Altogether the border around West Berlin was about a hundred and fifty-five kilometres long. Only around forty-three kilometres of that ran through the city between East and West Berlin. The rest separated West Berlin from the countryside of East Germany. West Berlin was an island, and the Wall surrounded it completely. After 1990 the Wall was taken down remarkably fast. Most of the concrete was crushed and used for roads. But hundreds of segments were sold or given away, and today you can find pieces of the Berlin Wall in cities all over the world, in parks, museums, and in front of embassies and company headquarters. Now look at the street sign. This street was renamed in 1951 after Käthe Niederkirchner, a young communist who fought against the Nazis and was murdered in the Ravensbrück concentration camp in 1944. The East German state named streets after resistance fighters to present itself as the anti-fascist Germany. Look across the street as well. The large sandstone building is the former Prussian House of Representatives. During the division it stood right next to the Wall, damaged and half empty. Since 1993 it has been the home of the Berlin state parliament, so the city's elected representatives now meet a few metres from where the Wall stood. If you have time, the Topography of Terror behind this segment is free to visit. Along the excavated cellar walls there's an open-air exhibition about the Gestapo, the SS and the police state they built. Standing here, between the remains of the Gestapo headquarters and the remains of the Wall, you can ask one of the questions this city is still asking: how does a society let this happen, and how does it remember it afterwards?

stops.title: Checkpoint Charlie
stops.text: Checkpoint Charlie got its name from the military alphabet. Alpha was at Helmstedt, on the inner German border, Bravo at Dreilinden, on the edge of Berlin, and this was Charlie. It was the crossing point for Allied soldiers, diplomats and foreigners. The booth and the soldiers you see today are for tourists. But in October 1961, this spot came very close to starting a war. East German border guards began demanding to see the papers of American officials, something the Allies refused to accept, since in their view only the Soviets had authority here. On the twenty-seventh of October, American tanks rolled up to the line. Soviet tanks answered on the other side. For about sixteen hours, American and Soviet tanks faced each other here, around a hundred metres apart, engines running and loaded with live ammunition. It ended through a quiet back channel between Kennedy and Khrushchev. One Soviet tank reversed, then one American tank, then another, until they were all gone. Now walk a little way east along Zimmerstrasse. On the seventeenth of August 1962, an eighteen-year-old bricklayer named Peter Fechter and his friend tried to climb the Wall near here. His friend made it. Fechter was shot in the hip and fell back into the death strip. He lay there for about fifty minutes, calling for help, while crowds in the West shouted and photographers took pictures. Neither the East German guards nor the American soldiers went to him. He bled to death. The images went around the world, and caused fury in West Berlin, including at the Americans. There's a small memorial column where he fell. Next is the longest ride of the tour, about four kilometres east to the East Side Gallery. You'll follow the old border along Zimmerstrasse, then cross the Spree at Jannowitzbrücke and ride along Holzmarktstrasse. The directions will guide you, so take your time and enjoy the ride.

more.text: Across the street from the checkpoint is a museum that has been here almost as long as the Wall itself. The Wall Museum was founded in 1962 by Rainer Hildebrandt, a human rights activist, and in 1963 it moved into a building right here, a few steps from the border. From its windows, people could watch the crossing and see the soldiers on both sides. The museum collected the ways people escaped, and many of them are astonishing. There were cars with hidden compartments behind the dashboard or under the back seat, and a tiny bubble car in which someone was hidden next to the engine. There were homemade diving equipment and small motors to pull swimmers across the water. In 1979 two families from Thuringia built a hot air balloon from bits of fabric, and at night they flew over the border into Bavaria. Some people escaped through the sewers, until the East installed grilles. Others simply used forged passports and tried to look calm. The border guards learned from every escape. Every successful attempt meant the checks became tighter. By the eighties, cars were examined with mirrors, dogs, and sometimes they were partly taken apart. The famous sign, You are leaving the American sector, written in English, Russian, French and German, stood here throughout the division. The original guard hut was lifted away by crane on the twenty-second of June 1990, in a ceremony attended by the foreign ministers of the four Allied powers and both German states. It's now in the Allied Museum in the south-west of Berlin, together with other objects from the American, British and French presence in the city. Look up at the large portraits of two young soldiers, one American and one Soviet. It's a photographic installation by the artist Frank Thiel from 1998. Each soldier looks towards the other's former sector. Today Checkpoint Charlie is one of the busiest tourist spots in Berlin, with souvenir shops and people in uniforms posing for photographs. Some Berliners find that uncomfortable. But try to imagine it as it was in October 1961, with tank engines running on both sides of the line, and the whole world waiting to see who would move first. It was the closest the Cold War came to turning hot in Berlin.

stops.title: The East Side Gallery
stops.text: You're now at the longest surviving stretch of the Berlin Wall, over thirteen hundred metres. But notice something: this wasn't the wall that faced the West. Here the border was the river Spree itself, behind the Wall. This was the inner wall, the one that faced East Berlin. Because Mühlenstrasse, the road you're on, was the route that official state guests took from the airport into the city, this wall was kept clean and grey, and East Berliners couldn't come near the other side. In 1990, after the fall, more than a hundred artists from around twenty countries painted it. The most famous painting shows two old men kissing. That's Leonid Brezhnev, leader of the Soviet Union, and Erich Honecker, leader of East Germany. It's based on a real photograph from 1979, during the thirtieth anniversary of the GDR. The socialist fraternal kiss was a real ritual between communist leaders. The artist, Dmitri Vrubel, called it something like: My God, help me to survive this deadly love. Look also for the little Trabant, East Germany's plastic people's car, bursting through the Wall. For East Germans, the Trabant was a symbol of their lives. People waited more than ten years to get one, and in November 1989, it became the car of freedom, as thousands of them drove into the West. This Wall has had to fight to survive even after 1989. Parts were removed to make way for luxury apartments in 2013, and thousands of people protested to protect it. Next, ride to the eastern end of the gallery, to the red brick bridge over the river. That's the Oberbaumbrücke.

more.text: When the artists came here in 1990, the Wall had only just opened. Many of them were from East Germany, and for the first time they could paint on a wall that had shut them in. Others came from all over the world. They worked fast, often with house paint, and the paintings were not designed to last. Over the years, weather, graffiti and souvenir hunters damaged the pictures badly. In 2009, for the twentieth anniversary of the fall of the Wall, the concrete was repaired and many of the original artists came back to repaint their own works. Some were unhappy about it, because the repainting erased years of history and layers of scribbled messages. Others were glad to see their work bright again. Look for a few of the pictures. The Trabant breaking through the Wall is called Test the Best, painted by Birgit Kinder. The number plate shows the date the Wall opened. Another shows a crowd of faces pouring through the Wall, and is called It happened in November. The artist, Kani Alavi, lived in a flat overlooking Checkpoint Charlie and watched the people flow through on the ninth of November. Walk around to the river side of the wall if you can. The area between the wall and the water was the border strip. On the other bank is Kreuzberg, which was West Berlin. From there, West Berliners could look over the river at this long grey wall and the watchtowers behind it. This part of the city has changed completely since then. The warehouses and factories along the river became clubs in the nineties, some of the most famous in Europe, on land nobody else wanted. Today much of it has been replaced by offices, hotels and a large concert arena, and the gallery is one of the last reminders of how empty this riverside once was. The Wall here is now a protected monument and part of the Berlin Wall Foundation. But it has always depended on people caring about it. When parts were removed for building projects, thousands of Berliners came out to protest, including the actor and musician David Hasselhoff, who famously sang at the Wall on New Year's Eve 1989. The painted wall you see is both a memorial and a living artwork, and it keeps changing.

stops.title: The Oberbaumbrücke
stops.text: This beautiful double-decker brick bridge, with its castle towers, was built in the eighteen-nineties. It connects Friedrichshain, in the East, with Kreuzberg, in the West. During the division, it was a border crossing, but only for pedestrians. From 1963, West Berliners could use crossings like this one to visit relatives in the East, at first only at Christmas, later on day passes. Imagine standing in a queue on this bridge, with your gifts, coffee and West chocolate, for a few hours with family you hadn't seen in years. Then going home before midnight. Now look at the water. The border here didn't run through the middle of the river. The entire width of the Spree belonged to East Berlin. The riverbank on the Kreuzberg side was West, but a single step into the water was East. Between 1966 and 1975, several young children from Kreuzberg fell into the river while playing on that bank. West Berlin police and firefighters were there within minutes, but they didn't dare go into the water, because that meant entering East German territory, where boats and guards were watching. The children drowned while adults stood helpless on the shore. The last was a five-year-old boy named Cengaver Katrancı, in 1975. After his death, East and West finally agreed on a rule allowing rescues in the border waters. Next, ride north up Warschauer Strasse to Frankfurter Tor, where two domed towers mark the start of Karl-Marx-Allee. Watch out for tram tracks on the way.

more.text: The name Oberbaum means upper tree, or upper beam. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries a large wooden boom, a tree trunk studded with nails, was stretched across the river here at night, so that no boat could enter the city without paying customs. The bridge kept the name. The bridge you see was finished in 1896, in a style that imitates a medieval city gate. The upper deck was built for one of Berlin's first elevated railway lines, which opened in 1902. You can see the arches of the track running along the top. In April 1945, in the last days of the war, German troops blew up the middle section of the bridge to slow the Soviet advance. For the next fifty years the bridge was damaged and divided. After 1961 the upper deck was empty, the trains cut off. After new agreements in the early seventies, West Berliners could visit the East more easily, and this bridge was one of the crossings they used, but only on foot. Every visitor had to exchange a fixed amount of West German marks into East German marks at a poor rate, and spend it in the East. You couldn't take the East German money home. After reunification the bridge was restored, and the destroyed middle section was replaced by a modern steel section designed by the Spanish architect Santiago Calatrava. In 1995 the trains returned to the upper deck. Today the U1 line runs over the bridge, and on a sunny day it's a wonderful place to watch the river. If you look downstream, towards the south-east, you'll see a giant aluminium sculpture of three figures standing in the water, full of holes. It's called Molecule Man, by the American artist Jonathan Borofsky. It stands where three districts meet, Kreuzberg, Friedrichshain and Treptow, two of them once in the East and one in the West. The figures seem to lean towards each other. The bridge also appears in the film Run Lola Run, from 1998, when Lola runs across it in her famous red hair. For many Berliners it has become the symbol of the city coming back together: a bridge between East and West, used every day by people who barely think about the fact that it was once a border.

stops.title: Karl-Marx-Allee
stops.text: Welcome to the grandest street in East Germany. It was originally called Stalinallee, and it was built in the fifties as the first socialist street in Germany, a showcase for the whole world to see. The two domed towers here at Frankfurter Tor were designed by the architect Hermann Henselmann, and they deliberately echo the domes of the French and German churches at Gendarmenmarkt. Look at the buildings. The style is sometimes called wedding cake style, with its columns, balconies and decorative ceramic tiles. These were called workers' palaces, and compared to the ruins that most Berliners were living in, they really were. They had central heating, lifts, hot water and parquet floors, luxuries at the time. But the building of this street had a dark side. It was the construction workers here, working under higher quotas and lower pay, who put down their tools on the sixteenth of June 1953 and started the uprising you heard about at the House of Ministries. Stalin also had his place here: a bronze statue of him stood on this avenue. In November 1961, after Moscow's final break with Stalin's memory, it disappeared overnight. The street was renamed Karl-Marx-Allee the same night. The avenue is almost ninety metres wide, and that width had a purpose: it was a parade route. Every year, on May Day and on the anniversary of the GDR, soldiers, tanks and missiles rolled past the leaders' tribune. Now ride west along Karl-Marx-Allee towards the TV tower. After Strausberger Platz, notice how the architecture changes into sixties modernism, with the Kino International cinema and Café Moskau. Your next stop is Alexanderplatz.

more.text: Stalinallee was more than a street. It was a promise. After the war, much of Berlin was rubble. The new East German state wanted to show that socialism would give ordinary workers better homes than capitalism ever had. In 1951 and 1952, thousands of volunteers helped clear the ruins here, often after their normal working day. Among those who helped, flats were later given out by lottery, so a bricklayer or a tram driver could end up living in one of these palaces. The buildings were made in the style the Soviet Union demanded at the time, called socialist classicism, with national decorative details. The architects studied old Berlin buildings from the time of the Prussian architect Schinkel, and added columns, cornices and the ceramic tiles you can see on the facades. In later decades the tiles began to fall off, and for years nets hung across parts of the buildings to protect people walking below. The Stalin statue that stood here was nearly five metres tall. When it was taken down in November 1961, it was done quietly at night. The story goes that a few small fragments were kept, and one of them, part of an ear, ended up on display in the Café Sibylle, a little further along this avenue, which has a small exhibition about the street's history. By the late fifties, the leadership decided the grand style was too expensive. The second half of the avenue, from Strausberger Platz towards Alexanderplatz, was built in the sixties with simpler, prefabricated panels. You're about to ride through that change, from wedding cake style into sixties modernism. Watch for the Kino International on the right as you ride. It opened in 1963 and was the cinema for official premieres. On the ninth of November 1989, it held the premiere of a film called Coming Out, the only East German feature film about gay life. When the audience came out of the cinema that night, they heard the news: the Wall was open. After reunification the flats were privatised and sold. Today this avenue is one of the most sought-after addresses in the east of the city, and the workers' palaces have become some of the most expensive flats in the neighbourhood. History here has a sense of humour.

stops.title: Alexanderplatz
stops.text: Look up at the TV tower. It's three hundred and sixty-eight metres high, and it was finished in 1969, to be seen from everywhere, including West Berlin. It was supposed to be a symbol of socialist modernity and technical progress. But when the sun hits the steel ball, the reflection forms a bright cross. Berliners immediately named it the Pope's revenge, a joke that the officially atheist state didn't enjoy. Nearby is the World Time Clock, also from 1969. It showed the time in cities all over the world, places most East Germans were never allowed to visit. Now picture this square on the fourth of November 1989. It's full of people, hundreds of thousands, maybe more. It's the largest demonstration in the history of East Germany, organised by actors and artists, and for the first time officially permitted. People carried handmade signs and jokes, and speakers called for freedom of speech, of the press, and of travel. One speaker was Günter Schabowski, a member of the Politburo, and the crowd booed him. Just five days later, on the evening of the ninth of November, the same Schabowski read out a new travel rule at a press conference, broadcast live. A journalist asked when it would take effect. Schabowski looked at his papers, confused, and said that as far as he knew, immediately. That night, thousands of East Berliners went to the border to test it, and the Wall opened. The whole system collapsed through a badly prepared press conference. Your last stop is at Bernauer Strasse, about three kilometres north-west. The directions will take you through the quiet side streets of Mitte.

more.text: Alexanderplatz is named after the Russian Tsar Alexander the First, who visited Berlin in 1805. For a long time it was a busy cattle market, and later a crossroads of trams, trains and department stores. In 1929 the writer Alfred Döblin made it famous with his novel Berlin Alexanderplatz, about a former convict trying to survive in the city. The square was badly damaged in the war, and in the sixties the East German state rebuilt it completely, as a wide, open centre for its capital, with space for crowds, parades and state celebrations. The TV tower was part of that plan. Look at the Haus des Lehrers, the House of the Teacher, near the tower. It's wrapped in a huge mosaic band called Our Life, by the artist Walter Womacka, showing scenes of work, science and family life in the socialist state. Now back to the fourth of November 1989. By then, the country was already shaking. In Leipzig, weekly Monday demonstrations had grown from a few hundred people to hundreds of thousands. Their chant was Wir sind das Volk, we are the people. Thousands of East Germans had fled through Hungary and through the West German embassy in Prague. The old leader, Erich Honecker, had been removed in October. At the demonstration here, the speakers included famous writers like Christa Wolf and Stefan Heym. Heym told the crowd that it was as if someone had opened a window after years of stale air. There was also Markus Wolf, the former head of East Germany's foreign intelligence service, who tried to present himself as a reformer. Many people booed. The signs were often funny. One of the most famous read: Visafrei bis Hawaii, visa-free to Hawaii. What makes that day so remarkable is that it was entirely peaceful. After decades of fear, hundreds of thousands of people stood on this square and said openly what they thought, and nobody was shot. The East German revolution of 1989 is sometimes called the peaceful revolution, and this was its high point in Berlin. Five days later the Wall opened. Less than a year after that, on the third of October 1990, East Germany ceased to exist, and Germany was reunited. The whole journey, from this square to the end of a state, took only eleven months.

stops.title: Bernauer Strasse
stops.text: You've reached the Berlin Wall Memorial, and this is the place where the Wall is easiest to understand. On Bernauer Strasse, the border ran along the front of the houses. The buildings on the south side were in the East, but the pavement in front of their doors was in the West. When the border was sealed in August 1961, people living here could step out of their front door into freedom, until the doors were bricked up. Then they jumped from the windows. West Berlin firefighters held out nets. Some made it, some didn't. On the twenty-second of August, fifty-eight-year-old Ida Siekmann threw her belongings out of her window at number forty-eight and jumped. She died of her injuries, one of the first people to die at the Wall. A little way down this street, on the fifteenth of August 1961, a young border guard named Conrad Schumann was standing at a coil of barbed wire. He looked around, threw his rifle away and jumped over the wire into the West. The photograph of that jump became one of the defining images of the Cold War. Later, the houses were emptied and torn down to widen the death strip. People dug tunnels under this street instead. In 1964, fifty-seven people escaped through a tunnel dug by students from a bakery on the western side. Look at the steel poles marking the line of the Wall, and at the Window of Remembrance, with the faces of people who died at the Berlin Wall. There are at least a hundred and forty of them. Climb the viewing tower at the documentation centre to see the preserved death strip from above. And one last detail: the chapel in the middle of the strip stands where the Church of Reconciliation once stood. It was trapped inside the death strip for over twenty years and blown up by East Germany in 1985. Four years later, the Wall itself was gone.

more.text: The line of steel poles you see marks where the Wall stood. It's part of a memorial stretching about one and a half kilometres along this street, and it tries to show the whole border strip, not just the Wall. Look out for the markers in the ground, which show where tunnels ran and where people died, and the original piece of the death strip preserved between two walls, with a watchtower still in place. The tunnels are one of the great stories of Bernauer Strasse. The soil here is sandy and the street is close to the border on both sides, so it was a good place to dig. Some tunnels were dug from the East, by people desperate to leave, and some from the West, by students and friends who wanted to bring people out. In 1962, a tunnel dug from a factory on the western side brought out twenty-nine people, and an American television network paid for part of the digging in exchange for the right to film it. The biggest was the one you heard about, Tunnel 57, in October 1964. Over two nights, fifty-seven people crawled through a tunnel about a hundred and forty metres long, from the backyard of a building on Strelitzer Strasse, in the East, to the old bakery in the West. On the second night, the Stasi found out. In the shooting that followed, a young East German border soldier named Egon Schultz was killed. The East blamed the escape helpers and made him a hero. Only after 1990 did the files show that he was most likely hit by a bullet fired by one of his own comrades. Look for the station entrance of Nordbahnhof nearby. It was another ghost station, closed and guarded under the border, while West Berlin trains passed through without stopping. The Chapel of Reconciliation, in the middle of the memorial, was built in 2000 out of rammed earth, mixed with fragments of the church that was blown up in 1985. On most weekdays at noon, a short service is held there to remember one person who died at the Berlin Wall, reading out their name and their story. Before you finish, climb the viewing tower at the documentation centre across the street. From up there you can see the preserved strip, the lights, the patrol road and the raked sand, exactly as border guards once saw it.

intro.title: Before you ride
intro.text: Welcome to Berlin, the city where the Cold War stopped being an idea and became a line of concrete through people's streets. Over the next two hours you'll ride about fifteen kilometres, from the Reichstag to the Berlin Wall Memorial at Bernauer Strasse, through eleven places where the division of Berlin was decided, enforced, resisted and finally broken. Each story plays by itself when you arrive, so you can keep your eyes on the road. A quick note on safety: Berlin's bike lanes are busy and fast. Keep one ear free, stop before you listen to the longer stories, and watch out for tram tracks, especially in the east. When you're ready, ride to the lawn in front of the Reichstag. Your first story starts there.

outro.title: End of the tour
outro.text: That's the end of the tour. In just fifteen kilometres, you've crossed the old border several times, something that for twenty-eight years could cost people their lives. If you still have energy, ride two kilometres north to the Bösebrücke on Bornholmer Strasse. That's where, on the night of the ninth of November 1989, the first gate was opened, when an overwhelmed officer named Harald Jäger decided to let the crowd through. Or head to the Mauerpark, on the former death strip, for a drink. Thanks for riding.

turnaround.text: Turn around when it is safe, then ride back to the route.

bonus.title: The Tränenpalast, the Palace of Tears
bonus.hint: About 900 metres east along the river. Afterwards, come back to the route at the Reichstag.
bonus.text: You're standing in front of a glass and steel pavilion next to Friedrichstrasse station. Berliners called it the Tränenpalast, the Palace of Tears. After 1961, Friedrichstrasse was the one station in the city centre where trains from East and West met. It sat entirely in East Berlin, but West Berlin S-Bahn and U-Bahn trains still stopped deep inside it, behind walls and passport controls. In 1962 East Germany built this hall as the departure point for people leaving the East for West Berlin. Mostly they were visitors from the West, going home after seeing family, and pensioners, who were allowed to travel. The East German relatives were not allowed to follow. So this was where families said goodbye. Outside the entrance, they hugged, cried and waved, not knowing when or whether they would see each other again. Inside, travellers queued for narrow control booths, one at a time, where border officers compared faces with passport photos, stamped papers and could order a search. The hall was used until the Wall opened in 1989. Since 2011 it has been a museum about everyday life at the border, and entry is free. If you have twenty minutes, go inside: you can walk through a reconstruction of the control booths. When you're ready, ride back along the river to the Reichstag and continue the tour to the Brandenburg Gate.

bonus.title: Bornholmer Strasse, where the Wall opened
bonus.hint: About 2 kilometres north of Bernauer Strasse, on the bridge over the railway.
bonus.text: This steel bridge over the railway tracks is the Bösebrücke, named after Wilhelm Böse, a resistance fighter executed by the Nazis in 1944. At its eastern end stood the border crossing at Bornholmer Strasse, and this is where the Berlin Wall first opened. On the evening of the ninth of November 1989, after Günter Schabowski's confused announcement on television, East Berliners began to gather here. Nobody at the checkpoint had any orders. The officer in charge that night was Harald Jäger, a lieutenant colonel of the Stasi's passport control unit. As the crowd grew into the thousands, chanting open the gate, he called his superiors again and again. They told him to let a few of the loudest people out, but to stamp their passports so that they could not come back, in effect expelling them without telling them. The crowd kept growing. Jäger feared that people would be crushed, or that someone would start shooting. At around half past eleven at night, on his own authority, he gave the order to open the barrier. Thousands of people poured across this bridge into the West, many of them laughing and crying at the same time. Within the next hours, the other crossings in the city opened too. One of the people who crossed here that night was a young physicist from East Berlin named Angela Merkel. She had been to the sauna, as she did every Thursday, and followed the crowd across the bridge. The square at the eastern end is now called Platz des Neunten November 1989. Look for the photographs and the markers of the old checkpoint. After twenty-eight years, the end of the Berlin Wall began right here, with one tired officer who decided not to shoot.
